extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners; PR managers and corporate communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and operating public relations programs addressing activist publics (environmental, consumer, minority), including choice of communication model, tactics, organizational structures, and research methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of communication model
rubrics_metrics.description: Select among press agentry/publicity, public-information, two-way asymmetric, and two-way symmetric models depending on goals and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four models differ substantially in philosophy and tactics. Press agentry often antagonizes activists; public-information can fail if orgs don't know what publics want; two-way asymmetric is persuasive tailoring to audience values (useful when publics are passive and organization controls messaging); two-way symmetric aims for negotiation and compromise (useful in policy arenas where mutual concessions are possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid whitewash publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on superficial promotional publicity ('whitewash') to make problems go away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press-agentry tactics (e.g., photos and boastful ads) typically antagonize activists — examples include Potlatch Forests' misleading ad and cosmetic minority-relations stunts. Simple positive portrayals without substantive change can backfire and deepen activist ire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the information publics want (not only what org wants to say)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give publics the kinds of information they seek rather than only promotional claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-information programs often fail because organizations haven't determined what information publics want to hear (example: utilities emphasized nuclear benefits but omitted dangers). Research publics to identify specific informational needs before rolling out education efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance positive messages with disadvantages (avoid appearing myopic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include disadvantages or trade-offs when presenting benefits; overemphasis on positives can make an organization appear blind to negative consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study of Army Corps of Engineers showed accurate benefit information without disadvantages made the Corps look myopic. Use coorientation methods to surface mismatches between public and organizational perceptions and to avoid omitting salient negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two-way asymmetric persuasion appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor messages to audience values and gather feedback to see if persuasion is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-way asymmetric can work when publics are passive and the organization largely controls the message. However, activist groups may use the same tactics, making it harder to control cognitions, attitudes, and behaviors. Avoid assuming unilateral influence in contested issue spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two-way symmetric communication to negotiate compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ symmetric, dialogic communication to find compromises between organizational and public interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication theorists (Paisley) and practitioners (Schacht) describe symmetric campaigns as negotiation/bargaining sessions that can produce compromises balancing conflicting needs (e.g., employment vs environment). Useful in policy arenas and when both sides have legitimate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforce audience values to persuade (hook messages to existing values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame messages by connecting with values the audience already holds rather than challenging them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peter Sandman's advice: 'The golden rule of persuasion is thus to look for existing audience values to which you can hook your message.' If opposing values exist, mention them less. Example values to hook: concerns about taxes, unmet social priorities, children's futures, love of places/people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify and repeat messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Pare complex technical explanations into manageable pieces and repeat core messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex explanations are hard to deliver and receive; industry advice: simplify, repeat, and emphasize themes the public can grasp (e.g., jobs at stake rather than profits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and opportunism
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a long-term presence and be ready to exploit opportunities opened by opponents' mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry counsel: 'Hang in there. Tides ebb and flow. Opportunities open up—for instance, following the Sierra Club debacle.' Persistence positions an organization to 'step in with your message' when advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be proactive rather than only reactive on environmental issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop ongoing environmental relations programs instead of waiting to respond to crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many organizations only launch environmental PR after challenges (e.g., Seabrook, Three Mile Island). Proactive programs can include reports (e.g., acid rain), speakers bureaus, and continuous outreach to anticipate and shape public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitize management to environmental concerns through face-to-face and multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct, immersive presentations and interpersonal contact to convince management of genuine environmental concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burson-Marsteller example: multimedia presentation to Gulf Oil executives showed pollution consequences. PR should 'impress on management the need to articulate genuine concern' and maintain continuing face-to-face communication with environmental critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a complaint system for consumer relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Create organized (often computerized) complaint-handling systems to channel consumer complaints to appropriate managers and subsystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaint systems provide early warnings about product issues and inform internal departments of adverse consequences (examples: Amoco for service stations; Ford for dealer escalation; Motorola for TV-set complaints). They can be a critical monitoring and corrective mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create interdepartmental consumer affairs committees with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up high-level, cross-department committees that can review and change policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AT&T's model includes VP-level interdepartmental committees empowered to review policies and make changes, improving responsiveness and aligning corporate policy with consumer interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consumer advisory panels and employee consumer panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate outside consumer representatives and employees into advisory bodies to surface consumer concerns and recommend changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AT&T used consumer advisory panels composed of consumer-organization reps and employee panels to inform top management about customer experiences and policy impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide consumer education and service innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer practical consumer services and educational materials to help consumers use products (e.g., unit pricing, open dating, nutritional labeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giant Food examples: unit pricing, open dating, nutritional labeling, percentage labeling. Such services can build consumer goodwill and reduce complaints; consult experts (e.g., nutritionists) when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as an internal consumer ombudsman/consultant
rubrics_metrics.description: Serve inside the company to advise departments about consumer difficulties (labels, packaging, displays) without imposing programs coercively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operating philosophy: 'never force a program on a particular department' — instead advise and suggest solutions based on shopper experiences and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liaise with consumer-interest organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain external relationships with consumer groups to monitor issues and coordinate responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational liaison keeps communication channels open with advocacy groups and can provide advance warning of emerging issues; participation in industry studies and associations supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement affirmative action and deliberate minority hiring steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Take deliberate steps to hire females and minority-group members, and comply with legal requirements when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative action is required for firms performing government subcontracts; even where not initially required, courts can mandate plans if discrimination is found. Use EEO Form 100 and other tracking to document and guide efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research minority community perceptions and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct targeted research to determine how the organization is regarded in minority communities and what media/publications influence them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D. Parke Gibson suggests identifying what the organization does that's of interest to specific minority groups, researching ethnic-oriented publications, and surveying minority-group leadership in relevant locations. Note that what interests one minority group may not interest another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in community participation and partnerships with minority institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop joint programs with schools and minority community organizations to build relationships and demonstrate commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: career opportunity days during community celebrations (Cinco de Mayo), PEPCO's outreach to predominantly black schools. Programs should emphasize dialogue and participation rather than one-way messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitization training sessions for management
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose managers to role-play or direct dialogue with minority leaders to force listening and awareness of grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training sessions where minority leaders play activists and confront managers can be a powerful first encounter, compelling managers to listen and engage with minority concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage grassroots/local media tactics to show local support
rubrics_metrics.description: Have local groups handle media relations, distribute leaflets, and emphasize local votes or opinions to portray campaigns as locally rooted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clamshell Alliance tactics included stressing local towns' votes, distributing thousands of leaflets at beaches, and encouraging local groups to handle media to show grassroots support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate operational/nonviolent tactics with authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform and coordinate with police and military authorities about plans (e.g., evacuation info, nonviolent civil disobedience leaflets) to portray movements as nonviolent and organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clamshell Alliance informed police of evacuation plans and distributed leaflets to National Guardsmen prior to occupation; such steps can reduce mischaracterization and build legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame activists' messages in audience-acceptable terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Couch demonstrations and demands in terms that will not alienate local residents and that resonate with audience concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: stressing evacuation risks, local voting records against nuclear power, and avoiding rhetoric that would alienate moderates; this is the asymmetric tactic of presenting the issue in audience-friendly frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coorientation methods to detect perception gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply coorientation research to compare what publics see as advantages/disadvantages with what the organization thinks publics perceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stamm and Bowes found publics recognized both advantages and disadvantages but predicted the Corps would see only advantages. Coorientation helps identify where organizations are missing salient public concerns and where communication needs to be adjusted.
